summary:
Neyra is a crop advisory tool developed by the ulugbek-crew for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in Tashkent under the Field Shift challenge. It's a simple promise: look before you plant.

It does not tackle the problem of bad weather. It’s poor information. Each farmer grows the crop that won last year. Everybody harvests during the same two weeks. The price goes through the floor. In April 2024, onions fell to 1,500 UZS per kg, about 4.4 times cheaper than the previous year. About 150,000-200,000 tons were dumped or fed to livestock.

Neyra is a web app and a Telegram bot, so a farmer can open it on a phone without installing anything. They mark a field, answer three questions, and get three crop options scored on four lights: water need in a dry year, whether it ripens before frost, soil benefit, and market and waste risk. Six crops are scored against 42 years of NASA POWER weather at that exact field.
details:
What it does

Neyra tells a farmer in Uzbekistan what to plant on a specific field before the season starts. The tagline is “see before you plant.”

The farmer marks their field on a map, answers three questions, and gets three crop options. Each option is scored on four lights: water need in a dry year, whether it ripens before frost, soil benefit from rotation, and market and waste risk. Six crops are scored against 42 years of NASA POWER weather at that exact point, not at the nearest city. Every number on screen carries the source it came from.

It runs two ways. There is a web app, and there is a Telegram bot, because Telegram is where Uzbek farmers already are. Nothing to install, no account, no cost.

How it works

Crop water need comes from FAO-56 Rev.1 reference evapotranspiration, computed from NASA POWER daily weather. Season length comes from growing degree days, then re-scaled against 767 field-years of MODIS phenology from MCD12Q2 v061. That calibration matters. The FAO reference table puts the end of season at 25 April. The satellite says 3 June. After calibration our model lands within half a day of the satellite. Soil moisture and groundwater context come from SMAP L4 and GRACE/GRACE-FO through NASA GIBS, shown as live layers on the farmer’s own field.

Benefits and intended impact

The waste in Uzbek agriculture is not mainly a weather problem. It is an information problem. Everyone plants last year’s winning crop, everyone harvests in the same two weeks, and the price collapses. In April 2024 onions sold for 1,500 UZS per kilogram, about 4.4 times below the year before, and 150,000 to 200,000 tonnes were dumped or fed to livestock. Across all fruit and vegetables, 20 to 30 percent of a roughly 23 million tonne crop is lost after harvest each year.

Those losses are deadweight loss in the strict sense. The land, the water, the seed and the labour were all spent, and no one consumed the output. Demand for onions barely moves with price, so a bigger crop is simply a crop nobody buys.

Water is the second target. Central Asia is water-constrained, and a crop that fails on price still drank its full irrigation allocation. Shifting the planting decision before the water is committed is far cheaper than any intervention after harvest.

The approach is regional, not national. Running the same onion model on NASA POWER for 1985 to 2025 puts Tashkent 30 days ahead of Turkistan in Kazakhstan and 62 days ahead of Volgograd in Russia. That is a harvest-window map for the whole region, and it works anywhere POWER has coverage.

Tools and technology

NASA data: POWER, MODIS through GIBS and EOSDIS, SMAP L4 soil moisture, GRACE and GRACE-FO, and MCD12Q2 v061 from ORNL DAAC. Agronomic methods from FAO-56 Rev.1 (2025), FAO-56 (1998) and FAO-29 Rev.1 (1985). Market figures from EastFruit, Kun.uz, Podrobno.uz and UzDaily. Mapping with Leaflet 1.9.4 on a Sentinel-2 cloudless basemap by EOX plus OpenStreetMap. The Telegram interface uses the Telegram Web Apps script. The code is open on GitHub and the site is hosted on Vercel. Every computed number is covered by tests. The logo is AI-generated. The layout, charts and numbers were built by hand from the sources above.

Creativity and what we considered

The creative turn was diagnostic. The obvious build is a weather forecaster. We found the real failure is coordination, so we built a decision tool instead of a prediction tool.

We also designed against the fallacy of composition. Advice that is right for one farmer is wrong if every farmer follows it, so the roadmap adds planted-area tracking with HLS 30 metre imagery, to warn when a crop is already crowded.

Neyra does not decide. The farmer decides, with evidence.
